lessons.title: Anatomy of Citrus Trees
lessons.body: A citrus tree has three main parts: roots, trunk, and canopy. The roots anchor the tree and absorb water and nutrients. Most feeder roots are in the top 30 cm of soil, spreading 1.5 times the canopy width. The trunk supports the canopy and transports water and nutrients. The canopy consists of branches, leaves, and fruit. Leaves are the factory: they capture sunlight for photosynthesis. Citrus leaves are evergreen, living 2-3 years. They are thick and waxy to reduce water loss. Flowers are small, white, and fragrant, appearing in spring. Fruit develops from the ovary after pollination. In Africa, common citrus types include sweet orange, mandarin, lemon, lime, and grapefruit. Grafting is common: a scion (fruit variety) is joined to a rootstock (e.g., rough lemon, trifoliate orange). Rootstocks affect tree size, disease resistance, and soil adaptation. For example, rough lemon rootstock is vigorous and suited to sandy soils, while trifoliate orange is dwarfing and tolerates cold. Knowing anatomy helps you prune, train, and diagnose problems. For instance, yellow leaves with green veins indicate iron deficiency, common in alkaline soils. Pruning opens the canopy for light and air, reducing disease. Remove water sprouts (vertical shoots) and suckers from the rootstock. In Africa, many farmers grow citrus in backyard orchards or small plots. Proper spacing (e.g., 5m x 5m for oranges) ensures good airflow. Understanding tree parts is the first step to good management.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Respiration in Citrus
lessons.body: Photosynthesis is how citrus trees make food. Leaves use sunlight, carbon dioxide (CO2), and water to produce sugars and oxygen. The process occurs in chloroplasts, mainly in the palisade cells of leaves. For every 6 molecules of CO2 and 6 of water, the tree makes 1 molecule of glucose and 6 of oxygen. Glucose is used for growth, fruit production, and stored as starch. Respiration is the opposite: trees break down sugars to release energy for growth and maintenance. This happens day and night, using oxygen and releasing CO2. The balance between photosynthesis and respiration determines net growth. If photosynthesis is low (e.g., due to shade, drought, or nutrient deficiency), growth and yield suffer. Citrus leaves are adapted to capture light efficiently. They have a waxy cuticle to prevent water loss and stomata (pores) on the underside for gas exchange. Stomata close when it's hot or dry to conserve water, which also reduces CO2 intake. In Africa, high temperatures and drought stress can limit photosynthesis. To maximize photosynthesis, ensure trees get full sun (at least 6 hours daily), adequate water (25-50 mm per week), and nutrients like nitrogen and magnesium (central to chlorophyll). Pruning to open the canopy improves light penetration. Avoid overhead irrigation in the evening, which can promote disease. Mulching conserves soil moisture and moderates temperature. Remember: healthy leaves = more sugar = more fruit. Monitor leaf color: dark green indicates good chlorophyll; yellowing signals problems. Test soil and leaf tissue for nutrients. With good management, a mature orange tree can produce 100-200 kg of fruit per year.

lessons.title: Growth Cycles and Phenology
lessons.body: Citrus trees have distinct growth cycles: flushes of new leaves, flowering, fruit set, and dormancy. In tropical Africa, growth can be continuous, but in subtropical areas (e.g., South Africa, Mediterranean North Africa), trees have 2-4 flushes per year, mainly in spring and summer. Flushes are periods of rapid shoot growth. New leaves are tender and light green, hardening over weeks. Flowering occurs after a period of cool temperatures (below 20Â°C) or drought stress, depending on variety. For example, oranges need 2-3 months of cool weather to induce flowering. In Kenya, flowering often happens at the start of the long rains (March-May). Fruit development takes 6-12 months, depending on type. Lemons and limes can flower and fruit year-round. Phenology is the timing of these events. It affects management: fertilize before flushes, irrigate during fruit set, and harvest at correct maturity. In Africa, climate variability can disrupt cycles. Drought delays flowering; too much rain during bloom reduces pollination. Keep records of flowering and harvest dates to plan operations. Pruning after harvest encourages new flush. Pests like citrus leafminer attack new flush. Monitor weekly. Use pheromone traps for fruit flies. Apply foliar sprays of zinc and boron during flush for healthy growth. A well-managed tree can have 3 flushes per year, each supporting future fruit. Understanding phenology helps you synchronize inputs with tree needs, leading to higher yields and better fruit quality.

lessons.title: Flowering and Fruit Development
lessons.body: Flowering is the start of fruit production. Citrus flowers are small, white, and fragrant. They can be perfect (male and female parts) or staminate (male only). Pollination is mostly by insects (bees) or wind. Some varieties, like mandarins, can set fruit without pollination (parthenocarpy). Flowering is triggered by cool temperatures (15-20Â°C) or water stress. In Africa, many farmers induce flowering by withholding irrigation for 4-6 weeks, then watering heavily. After pollination, the ovary develops into fruit. Initially, many small fruits form, but most drop (June drop) due to competition. Only 1-5% of flowers become mature fruit. Fruit growth follows a sigmoid curve: slow, fast, then slow. It takes 6-12 months to mature. For oranges, 7-9 months; lemons, 5-7 months. Fruit size and quality depend on water, nutrients (especially potassium), and sunlight. During development, ensure consistent moisture; drought causes fruit drop and small size. Apply potassium sulfate (e.g., 200g per tree per year) to improve fruit size and sweetness. Pest control is critical: fruit flies lay eggs in young fruit, causing rot. Use bait sprays or traps. Harvest when fruit reaches maturity: color change (e.g., green to orange), juice content (e.g., 40% for oranges), and sugar-acid ratio. In Africa, market demand often favors early harvest, but immature fruit is sour and reduces repeat sales. Test with a refractometer (Brix) and acid titration. Proper handling after harvest extends shelf life. With good management, a mature tree can produce 50-150 kg of fruit per season.

lessons.title: Root Systems and Nutrient Uptake
lessons.body: Citrus roots are shallow, with most feeder roots in the top 30 cm of soil. They spread horizontally up to 1.5 times the canopy diameter. Roots absorb water and nutrients, and anchor the tree. They also store carbohydrates. Root health is crucial: compacted or waterlogged soils suffocate roots. In Africa, many soils are sandy or clayey, affecting root growth. Sandy soils drain fast but leach nutrients; clay soils hold water but can become waterlogged. Improve soil with organic matter (compost, manure) to enhance structure and nutrient holding. Citrus needs 12 essential nutrients: macronutrients (N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S) and micronutrients (Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo, Cl). Nitrogen (N) promotes leaf and shoot growth. Phosphorus (P) supports root and flower development. Potassium (K) improves fruit size, color, and juice quality. Calcium (Ca) strengthens cell walls. Magnesium (Mg) is central to chlorophyll. Micronutrients like zinc and iron are needed in small amounts but are often deficient in African soils, especially alkaline ones. Nutrient uptake is affected by soil pH. Citrus prefers pH 5.5-6.5. At higher pH, iron, zinc, and manganese become unavailable, causing yellowing. At lower pH, aluminum toxicity can occur. Test soil annually. Apply fertilizers based on soil test and leaf analysis. For a mature orange tree, apply 1-2 kg of NPK 2:1:1 per year, split into 3-4 applications. Foliar sprays of zinc and manganese during flush correct deficiencies quickly. Over-fertilizing can burn roots and pollute groundwater. Use organic sources like manure (10-20 kg per tree per year) to improve soil health. Mulching conserves moisture and reduces weeds. Proper irrigation (drip or basin) ensures nutrients dissolve and reach roots. Healthy roots = healthy tree.

lessons.title: Hormonal Regulation in Citrus
lessons.body: Hormones are chemical messengers that control citrus growth and development. The main hormones are auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid, and ethylene. Auxins promote root formation and apical dominance (suppress side shoots). Gibberellins stimulate shoot elongation and delay fruit aging. Cytokinins promote cell division and delay leaf senescence. Abscisic acid (ABA) closes stomata during drought and promotes seed dormancy. Ethylene ripens fruit and promotes leaf and fruit drop. In citrus, hormones regulate flowering, fruit set, and drop. For example, gibberellic acid (GA3) sprays can reduce fruit drop and improve rind quality. Auxins like 2,4-D can prevent pre-harvest drop but must be used carefully to avoid residues. Ethylene is used commercially to degreen lemons and oranges. In Africa, smallholders can use simple techniques: pruning alters auxin distribution, promoting branching. Water stress increases ABA, inducing flowering. Fruit thinning (removing excess young fruit) reduces competition and increases size, mediated by hormones. Hormones also interact with nutrients. For instance, nitrogen promotes cytokinin synthesis, boosting growth. Zinc deficiency reduces auxin production, causing little leaf and dieback. Understanding hormones helps you manipulate trees for better yield. Use GA3 (10-20 ppm) at fruit set to reduce June drop. Apply ethephon (an ethylene releaser) to accelerate fruit ripening for early market. But always follow label instructions. Overuse can harm trees and environment. Integrated management combines pruning, irrigation, nutrition, and judicious hormone use. For African farmers, low-cost options like pruning and water management are often sufficient. Record observations: note when natural drop occurs, and plan interventions. With practice, you can use hormones to your advantage.

quiz.q: What is the primary function of citrus leaves?
quiz.explanation: Leaves contain chlorophyll and are the main site of photosynthesis, producing sugars for the tree.

quiz.q: Which rootstock is known for dwarfing and cold tolerance?
quiz.explanation: Trifoliate orange is a common rootstock that reduces tree size and improves cold hardiness.

quiz.q: What does the waxy cuticle on citrus leaves do?
quiz.explanation: The waxy cuticle is a protective layer that limits transpiration and water loss from the leaf surface.

quiz.q: Which part of the tree is responsible for water and nutrient uptake?
quiz.explanation: Feeder roots, mostly in the top 30 cm of soil, absorb water and dissolved nutrients.

quiz.q: What is the ideal spacing for orange trees in an orchard?
quiz.explanation: 5m x 5m spacing allows adequate light, airflow, and root space for mature orange trees.

quiz.q: What are the products of photosynthesis?
quiz.explanation: Photosynthesis uses CO2 and water to produce glucose (sugar) and oxygen.

quiz.q: When do stomata typically close?
quiz.explanation: Stomata close to conserve water when it is hot and dry, reducing CO2 intake and photosynthesis.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is central to chlorophyll and photosynthesis?
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen is a key component of chlorophyll, the pigment that captures light for photosynthesis.

quiz.q: What is the recommended weekly water requirement for citrus?
quiz.explanation: Citrus trees generally need 25-50 mm of water per week for optimal growth and fruit production.

quiz.q: What does a dark green leaf indicate?
quiz.explanation: Dark green leaves typically indicate adequate chlorophyll and nitrogen, showing good health.

quiz.q: What is a flush in citrus?
options: A) A period of rapid shoot growth
quiz.explanation: A flush is a period of rapid new leaf and shoot growth, common in spring and summer.

quiz.q: In subtropical Africa, what triggers flowering in oranges?
options: B) Cool temperatures or drought stress
quiz.explanation: Oranges require a period of cool temperatures (below 20Â°C) or water stress to induce flowering.

quiz.q: How long does it take for an orange fruit to mature?
quiz.explanation: Oranges typically take 7-9 months from flowering to mature fruit, depending on variety and climate.

quiz.q: What is the June drop?
options: B) Natural fruit drop due to competition
quiz.explanation: June drop is the natural shedding of excess young fruit to balance the tree's resources.

quiz.q: Which nutrient improves fruit size and sweetness?
quiz.explanation: Potassium is essential for fruit development, improving size, color, and sugar content.

quiz.q: What percentage of citrus flowers typically become mature fruit?
quiz.explanation: Only a small fraction (1-5%) of flowers set fruit that reaches maturity due to natural drop.

quiz.q: What is parthenocarpy?
quiz.explanation: Parthenocarpy is the production of fruit without fertilization, common in some mandarins.

quiz.q: What tool can measure fruit sugar content?
quiz.explanation: A refractometer measures Brix, which indicates the sugar content of fruit juice.

quiz.q: Where are most citrus feeder roots located?
quiz.explanation: The majority of feeder roots are in the top 30 cm of soil where oxygen and nutrients are available.

quiz.q: What soil pH range is ideal for citrus?
quiz.explanation: Citrus prefers slightly acidic soil with pH 5.5-6.5 for optimal nutrient availability.

quiz.q: Which deficiency causes yellowing with green veins?
quiz.explanation: Iron deficiency, common in alkaline soils, causes interveinal chlorosis (yellow leaves with green veins).

quiz.q: What is the recommended annual NPK application for a mature orange tree?
quiz.explanation: A mature orange tree typically requires 1-2 kg of NPK fertilizer per year, split into applications.

quiz.q: Which hormone promotes root formation?
quiz.explanation: Auxins are hormones that stimulate root initiation and apical dominance.

quiz.q: What does abscisic acid (ABA) do during drought?
quiz.explanation: ABA signals stomatal closure to reduce water loss when the plant experiences drought stress.

quiz.q: Which hormone is used to degreen citrus fruit?
quiz.explanation: Ethylene is used commercially to degreen citrus fruits, enhancing their color.

quiz.q: What is the effect of gibberellic acid (GA3) on fruit?
quiz.explanation: GA3 sprays can reduce pre-harvest fruit drop and improve rind quality.

quiz.q: How can smallholders induce flowering naturally?
quiz.explanation: Water stress (withholding irrigation for 4-6 weeks) followed by heavy watering can induce flowering.

quiz.q: What is apical dominance?
options: A) Suppression of side shoots by the terminal bud
B) Death of the main stem
quiz.explanation: Apical dominance is the phenomenon where the main apical bud suppresses the growth of lateral buds.

quiz.q: Which micronutrient is often deficient in African alkaline soils?
quiz.explanation: Zinc deficiency is common in alkaline soils, causing little leaf and interveinal chlorosis.

quiz.q: What is the role of cytokinins in citrus?
quiz.explanation: Cytokinins promote cell division and delay leaf senescence, supporting growth.
